content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work presents a new benchmark for RL agents working in a multimodal environment with visual and text inputs. Text is expressed in natural language. The benchmark consists of agents placing or removing objects in the environment. One of the main complexities is that the agent has to give the exact coordinates and features of the object that is placing or removing. Thus, the action space in the free version of the benchmark is more than 1e6 actions. Once the agent believes it is fulfilling the txt specification it has to send a stop action

To guide the agents the benchmark has scripted functions that penalize the agent if it tries to do something not allowed in the current state, e.g., overlapping two objects or removing an object that is not in the environment (or in the coordinates given). Since the PPO struggle in this environment, specially in the free positioning, authors do some feature engineering by masking all the actions but stop when the agent needs to take the stop action. They call this variant PPO+SF.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Compositional learning of natural language instructions in grounded agents is a notably challenging and relevant problem in RL. The benchmark is quite complex and clearly a product of hard work.

However, I believe that this work has too many weaknesses at this point that need to be tackled before being considered for publication:
1) It lacks motivation about why is this benchmark a good contribution compared to existing ones, (MiniGrid, MiniWorld or MiniHack). What does this benchmark require from an intelligent agent that cannot be achieved from the existing ones? 
2) Despite being so complex on its action space, it has a significantly smaller number of shapes and colours than other benchmarks. Previous studies of compositional generalisation  in RL highlighted that most RL agents will overfit with so little variety of figures [1,2]. It is also known that an egocentric perspective is key for compositional reasoning in RL [1,2]. However this benchmark, despite targeting compositional generalisation for RL, doesn't allow that kind of perspective.
3) The benchmark is very rigid. For the version introduced here, authors required large human notations (and spent several thousand dollars on it) to be able to tell when thee agent has fulfilled a task. This suggests that extending this benchmark with new shapes and colours or tasks won't be trivial as in existing alternatives.
4) It claims that one of it main features is providing human-written instructions. Yet all the instructions given as example follow a very schematic structure, e.g., all start with a "there is". If all instructions start like that it becomes irrelevant information (this is the reason why other benchmark go for tasks like "black triangle on top of blue cube"). It is not evident if the additional "naturality" of the instructions are really meaningful for the task itself.
5) Following the point above, even when the work only points to natural language, it resembles benchmarks and assumptions from existing literature on RL agents following instructions in temporal logic [2-4]. I believe it would be valuable to contrast this work at least with [4].
6) I believe the paper needs to motivate better the design choices, they usually lack to answer why?.  For instance, why is it better to have 1e6 action space rather than having the objects being pushed around? Why only two configurations Tower and Scatter? if they are just about difficulty levels, it sems quite abrupt to have one action space of 13 and other 1e6, it would be good to have some intermediate steps.
7) The benchmark requires a lot of supervision, about what actions are needed, when to stop, etc. I wonder if it won't be more suited to focus more on supervised learning instead. 
8) Some parts of the paper are not self-contained, e.g., NVLR is referred but not well explained -it assumes the reader is familiar with it-, e.g.  section 4.1 starts saying "NVLR includes human-written natural language statements paired with synthetic images" are the statements and images the same of your example? it seems not, since authors had to do additional programming and labelling but this is not clear. The acronym also is never detailed. 


[1] Hill, Felix, et al. "Environmental drivers of systematicity and generalization in a situated agent." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2020.
[2]León, Borja G., Murray Shanahan, and Francesco Belardinelli. "Agent, do you see it now? systematic generalisation in deep reinforcement learning." ICLR Workshop on Agent Learning in Open-Endedness. 2022.
[3]Andreas, J., Klein, D., and Levine, S. Modular multitask reinforcement learning with policy sketches.377
In Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning-Volume 70, pp. 166–175.378 JMLR. org, 2017.
[4]Camacho, Alberto, et al. "LTL and Beyond: Formal Languages for Reward Function Specification in Reinforcement Learning." IJCAI. Vol. 19. 2019.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I believe the paper is mostly easy to follow. Still and the part about the NVLR dataset is not self-contained. Also the related work section appears to early in my opinion, it contrast the work with existing ones before presenting it, which makes the reader to go back and forth. I think it would be better placed right before the conclusions. 

Many points lack motivation. There is not theoretical ground on what skills this benchmark requires wrt existing ones except for the ability to tackle a large action space. To tackle this, authors do some feature engineering like coarser grids, although they also mention that using this many MDPs become unsolvable (without giving much explanation).

The benchmark is similar to existing ones with the main difference of the action space and that the agent is not within the environment. still, authors fail to provide motivation on why this is relevant.

About reproducibility, authors state that the code will be released upon publication.
content.summary_of_the_review: Complex benchmark that fails to capture some of the most important features for compositionality in RL. It also needs better comparison and motivation wrt existing benchmarks. It is also difficult to customize for future research and in general. I am afraid it also requires to work bettr on justify what new features of intelligence is trying to grasp.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper introduces a new benchmark for RL where states consist in 2D collections of abstract objects (circles, triangles, squares) in different colors and sizes, and the reward function is described by a natural language statement. The statements are paired with human-annotated Python programs that enable exact computation of the reward function in any possible state.

The authors implement two baselines (PPO and PPO with "stop forcing"), each paired with one of two possible neural network architectures (BERT+CNN and ViLT), showing good results on simple cases but much worse results on the most challenging cases.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: the authors do a thorough job at designing a new benchmark which appears to be challenging based on the shown results. Details on how the benchmark was designed and created are very clear in the paper.

Weaknesses: the proposed task is somewhat still limited in variability and not particularly realistic. This is particularly true for the "Tower" variant, where it shouldn't be difficult for a visual model to transform the input image into a discrete description of the state, and solve the RL+language part of the task completely separately from the visual part. The "Scatter" variant instead seems more diverse and it looks like it features a more interesting interaction between visual scene, natural language statement, and action space (e.g., Figure 1 has a statement where the task is to place objects near each other).

Here are two concrete actionable points based on the feedback above.

1. It would be nice if the paper discussed the interaction of different modalities in the different variants of the benchmark. The model needs to learn to parse the visual scene, understand the natural language statement, and figure out how to solve the task. Are these three necessarily entangled with each other, or do we expect a successful model to do these three things separately? There doesn't need to be a definitive answer, but a discussion would be nice.

2. In my opinion, it would be useful to run the baselines on the same benchmark where we the states are described not as visual scenes but through the underlying compact representation. For instance, in the "Tower" variant, a state can be encoded as a 3x4x4 tensor of zeros and ones (3 components for the boxes, 4 components for the positions of a square within a box, and 4 possibilities for the color or "no square"). Results on this simplified benchmark would help us understand to what extent the task difficulty should be attributed to parsing the visual modality.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is written very clearly. It introduces a benchmark which is novel and potentially useful for the community.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the contribution is good but it does not particularly stand out. I am slightly leaning towards a rejection, but I am willing to change my recommendation if my comments are properly addressed.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work creates a reinforcement learning benchmark for natural language visual reasoning. The benchmark makes use of the NLVR corpus (Suhr et al., 2017), which contains massive pairs of natural statements grounded in synthetic images. The agent adds and removes objects conditioned on a natural language statement to modify the environment. The goal is for the environment to match up with a given natural language statement. Experiments on the benchmark show that existing models can provide non-trivial performance, while there remains significant room for improvement.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
> Strength

The description of how the benchmark is created is generally clear enough.

The proposed benchmarks have relatively rich state spaces and diverse semantic complexity. Each language statement is paired with multiple start states and reward functions to form thousands of MDPs of varying difficulty.

Extensive human annotation allows accurate computing of semantic rewards. The Python programs are executable in a structured representation of the environment and allow for exact and reliable reward computation at every possible state.

> Weaknesses

A brief overview of existing benchmarks could be added to better illustrate the motivation of the proposed benchmark.

A key challenge in language-conditioned RL benchmarks is to parse semantics for reward computing. The authors address this by annotating all statements with Python programs. However, this method may be costly and has high demands on the annotator. In addition, some ablation studies can be added to the experimental chapter to show that the reward calculation (Section 3) is superior.

More baselines can be used on this benchmark. For instance, the best performing model on NLVR corpus (Suhr et al., 2017) can be considered to extract the image and text features. Also, more quantitative analysis can be added to the experimental section to compare the differences between expert rewards and baselines.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, despite the fact that there is potential for improvement in this work, I believe this benchmark contributes to the field.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
